q: What is proprioception?
options: How quickly you respond to a stimulus
The body's ability to sense its position in space without looking
The maximum oxygen the body can use
explanation: Proprioception lets you sense your body's position without looking, like walking in the dark. Responding quickly is reaction time; smoothness is fluidity.

q: What is coordination training?
options: Exercises that only build muscle size
Exercises that help muscles, joints, eyes, and brain work together so movements become smoother, faster, and more accurate
explanation: Coordination training synchronizes movement patterns using muscles, joints, eyes, and brain, improving timing, rhythm, and control.

q: What is functional training?
options: Exercises that replicate or simulate real-life movements to make daily tasks easier, safer, and more efficient
explanation: Functional training mimics real-life movements like walking, lifting, reaching, climbing, and sit-to-stand. Its goal is not looks or athletic performance.

q: What is a standard Tabata protocol?
options: 30 seconds work, 15 seconds rest, 6 rounds, 4.5 minutes
40 seconds work, 20 seconds rest, 8 rounds, 8 minutes
20 seconds work, 10 seconds rest, 8 rounds, 4 minutes
60 seconds work, 30 seconds rest, 4 rounds, 6 minutes
explanation: Classic Tabata is 8 rounds of 20 seconds all-out work and 10 seconds rest, totaling 4 minutes.

q: What is EPOC?
options: Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption, the extra oxygen the body takes in after a workout to recover
explanation: EPOC is the extra oxygen used after a workout to repair, cool down, and recover. It is called the Afterburn Effect.

q: What is VO2 max?
options: The maximum amount of oxygen your body can take in and use during exercise
The highest heart rate you can reach
The longest time you can exercise
The number of rounds in a Tabata
explanation: VO2 max is the limit of your aerobic engine: the maximum oxygen you can take in and use during exercise.

q: What is supra-maximal high-intensity interval training (SMIT)?
options: Training at 50% to 70% of VO2 max
Brief, all-out bursts above 100% of VO2 max with passive or light recovery
explanation: SMIT bursts exceed 100% of VO2 max (130% to 170%+). Supra-maximal means above maximum. True Tabata is a SMIT protocol.

q: What does PGC-1α do?
options: It stores lactate in the muscles
It lowers heart rate during rest
It acts as the master switch for mitochondrial biogenesis, signaling cells to build new mitochondria
explanation: PGC-1α is the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis. More mitochondria mean faster oxygen processing and waste clearing.

q: In which plane do side-to-side movements like lateral lunges and skater hops occur?
explanation: The frontal plane divides front from back, and side-to-side movement happens in it.

q: In which plane do rotational movements like Russian twists occur?
explanation: The transverse plane divides the body horizontally and contains rotational and twisting movement.

q: Which foundational movement pattern is a kettlebell deadlift?
options: Hinge, a hip-dominant pattern with a neutral spine
explanation: The deadlift is a hip hinge that loads the glutes and hamstrings with little knee travel compared with a squat.

q: What is the role of local core stabilizers like the transversus abdominis and multifidus?
options: Producing fast spinal flexion during sit-ups
Being the main movers for rotational power
Stiffening each spinal segment and firing before the limbs move to protect the spine
Moving the femur in hip exercises
explanation: Local (tonic) stabilizers fire feed-forward to stiffen spinal segments before limb movement.

q: What were the results of the 1996 Tabata study after 6 weeks?
options: Steady-state VO2 max rose about 10% with no anaerobic gain; Tabata VO2 max rose 14% and anaerobic capacity 28%
Both groups improved only anaerobic capacity
Steady-state improved more in both areas
explanation: The Tabata group improved both VO2 max (14%) and anaerobic capacity (28%), while the steady-state group gained about 10% VO2 max and nothing anaerobic.

q: How did Group 1 (moderate-intensity steady-state) train in the 1996 study?
options: 5 days a week, 60 minutes at 70% of VO2 max
3 days a week, 30 minutes at 50% of VO2 max
explanation: The MISS group trained 5 days a week for 60 minutes at 70% of VO2 max. The Tabata group sprinted at 170% of VO2 max.

q: Which three things does the body do during EPOC after a Tabata session?
options: Builds fat, raises temperature, releases more catecholamines
Stops all metabolism, lowers oxygen use, stores lactate
Replenishes ATP and phosphocreatine, converts lactate back into glucose, lowers core temperature and clears catecholamines
Grows bones, lengthens muscles, improves eyesight
explanation: EPOC refills ATP and PCr stores, recycles lactate into glucose in the liver, and cools the body while clearing stress hormones.

q: What are the MMFIT intensity and time for balance training?
explanation: Balance training is light to moderate (RPE 3 to 5), 10 to 20 minutes, often as part of a warm-up or cooldown.

q: What are the MMFIT intensity and frequency for functional training?
options: Moderate, RPE 5 to 7, 3 to 5 times a week
Light, RPE 1 to 2, once a week
Light to moderate, RPE 3 to 6, 2 to 4 times a week
explanation: Functional training is moderate (RPE 5 to 7), 3 to 5 times a week, 15 to 30 minutes. RPE 3 to 6, 2 to 4 times a week is coordination training.

q: How does standard HIIT differ from SMIT in intensity?
options: HIIT is 130% to 170% of VO2 max; SMIT is 50% to 60%
HIIT is 80% to 95% of VO2 max with 1 to 4 minute intervals; SMIT is 130% to 170%+ with 10 to 30 second bursts
HIIT has no rest; SMIT has no work
explanation: HIIT pushes near the limit (80% to 95% VO2 max). SMIT goes beyond it (130% to 170%+), so bursts last only 10 to 30 seconds.

q: What is the correct order of energy phases during the 8 Tabata rounds?
options: Alactic (rounds 1 to 2), glycolytic (rounds 3 to 5), oxidative peak (rounds 6 to 8)
explanation: Stored ATP and PCr run out by round 2, glycolysis surges in rounds 3 to 5, and the aerobic system peaks in rounds 6 to 8.

q: Right after phosphocreatine runs out in round 2 of a Tabata, what does the body rely on next?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis, breaking down glycogen without oxygen
explanation: In rounds 3 to 5 the body turns to anaerobic glycolysis, raising blood lactate and causing the muscle burn.

q: Which list orders the training types from lowest to highest intensity?
explanation: Steady-state is sub-maximal, HIIT is 80% to 95% VO2 max, and SMIT is 130% to 170%+, like 60, 100, and 160 mph in the car analogy.

q: What is the order of the three parts of a Tabata as a SMIT protocol?
options: Burst (20 s at about 170% VO2 max), recovery (10 s passive rest), accumulation (repeated over 8 rounds)
explanation: Each round is a 20-second burst then 10 seconds of passive rest, and the 8 rounds accumulate until the aerobic engine redlines.

q: Which is NOT one of the three hallmarks of an elite-level metabolic intervention?
options: Long, comfortable sessions of 45 to 60 minutes
explanation: Long, comfortable sessions describe a regular workout. The hallmarks are supra-maximal intensity, mitochondrial biogenesis, and EPOC.

q: Which pairing of an exercise and its plane is mismatched?
explanation: A lateral lunge moves side to side, so it is in the frontal plane, not the transverse plane.

q: Which exercise is NOT suitable for a true Tabata, according to the lesson?
explanation: Single-joint isolation exercises like bicep curls do not recruit enough muscle to demand 170% of VO2 max.

q: Which pairing of a balance concept and its meaning is mismatched?
options: Stability: staying upright and steady when your center of gravity shifts
Control: how quickly you respond to a stimulus
Core: muscles of the abdomen, lower back, hips, and pelvis
Proprioception: sensing your position without looking
explanation: Control is how well you manage your movements: slow, deliberate, and precise. Responding quickly to a stimulus is reaction time.

q: Which statement about a regular workout versus an elite metabolic intervention is NOT true?
options: An elite intervention can be as short as 4 minutes
An elite intervention works both aerobic and anaerobic engines
A regular workout causes a high biological shock that forces rapid cellular remodeling
explanation: A regular workout causes low to moderate disruption. The high biological shock describes an elite intervention like true Tabata.

q: A student doing Tabata air squats has tight ankles: the heels lift and the torso tips forward. What is the best regression?
options: Squat faster to bypass the restriction
Elevate the heels on small plates or wedges, or use a box squat
Round the lower back to balance
explanation: Raising the heels makes up for limited ankle dorsiflexion and keeps the torso upright; a box squat also helps.

q: A coach watches heart rate monitors in the first two Tabata rounds and sees heart rates still low, then decides students are not working hard. Why is this reasoning wrong?
options: Heart rate drops to zero during sprints
Heart rate sensors cannot read above 100 bpm
Heart rate lags behind the real effort (cardiac inertia), so RPE or power output is a better guide early on
explanation: Heart rate takes about 45 to 90+ seconds to catch up with short, intense bursts, so it understates effort in early rounds.

q: A student loves Tabata and does a maximal full-body session every single day with no rest days. Weeks later she has a high resting heart rate and trouble sleeping. What is the likely cause?
options: Sympathetic overtraining from too much high-intensity work without recovery
Her VO2 max fell to zero
explanation: Daily maximal Tabata without recovery overloads the nervous and hormone systems, causing sympathetic overtraining with high resting heart rate and poor sleep.
